catalog_quote: Word stress for nouns, adjectives, and prepositions places the greatest degree of stress on the rightmost syllable of the word. Similarly, phrasal stress places the most prominent
sweep_summary: Two title hits for dari1249. (1) Bing 1980 (Linguistic Inquiry) is the catalog's deciding source and is already. re-read in full from the ODU-deposited scan: word stress on nouns/adjectives/prepositions falls on the final (rightmost) syllable, predictable from syllable count (pp.438, 444); ezafe never stressed, enclitics and inflectional suffixes destressed (pp.444-446); verbs stress the initial syllable (fn.7, p.445). Confirms the fixed-strict/final coding; nothing new supersedes it. our earlier reading's downloaded JIPA Illustration (Baker 2016, p.232, says the same. (2) Dilley, Shattuck-Hufnagel & Ostendorf 1996 (Journal of Phonetics) is a Glottolog misattribution: its abstract (Semantic Scholar/Crossref) describes glottalization of word-initial vowels in an FM-radio-news corpus (American English); not about Dari, priority none, and it should be removed from the Dari bibliography where it is currently listed. No open full text of Dilley was downloaded (ScienceDirect 403; not needed).

new_statements.quote: Word stress for nouns, adjectives, and prepositions places the greatest degree of stress on the rightmost syllable of the word. Similarly, phrasal stress places the most prominent stress on the rightmost word in noun phrases, adjective phrases, and prepositional phrases. [fn.7, p.445:] ... it will be necessary to make some provision to prevent rule (3) from applying to verbs and verb phrases, since stress tends to fall on the initial syllable of verbs and on the word preceding the verb in the verb phrase.
new_statements.citation: Bing, Janet Mueller (1980). Linguistic Rhythm and Grammatical Structure in Afghan Persian. Linguistic Inquiry 11(3): 437-463.
new_statements.locator: p.444, sec.3 first sentence; p.445 fn.7 (verbs)
new_statements.reading: Fixed final-syllable word stress on nouns, adjectives and prepositions, predictable from syllable count with no morphological conditioning; ezafe, pronominal enclitics and inflectional suffixes are unstressed; finite verbs stress the initial syllable (prefix). This is the catalog's own deciding source, re-read in the copy we hold; every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated pages, and it supports the fixed-strict (final) coding, with the verb pattern as a lexical-category exception rather than a counterexample to fixed final stress.

sources.citation: Bing, Janet Mueller (1980). Linguistic Rhythm and Grammatical Structure in Afghan Persian. Linguistic Inquiry 11(3): 437-463.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.438: 'Word stress for these categories is predictable, independent of the apparent structure of the word. Regardless of whether a word is apparently derived from other words ..., is borrowed from another language ..., or has no obvious morphological boundaries ..., the stress pattern can be predicted from the number of syllables the word contains.' ... 'For words of two syllables, the labeling of the metrical tree is obvious, since the greatest degree of stress falls on the final syllable of the words in question'. p.444: 'Word stress for nouns, adjectives, and prepositions places the greatest degree of stress on the rightmost syllable of the word.'
sources.locator: p.438 (sec.1 'Word Stress for Nouns, Adjectives, and Prepositions in Dari'); p.444 (sec.3); p.445 fn.7; pp.444-446 (enclitics/suffixes). Data: educated Kabul speakers, transcriptions from Entezar (1964) checked with informants (p.437-438).
sources.note: Primary stress on the final syllable of nouns, adjectives and prepositions, predictable from syllable count with no cyclic/morphological conditioning (examples maelem 'teacher', zendaegi 'life', aspaezxanae 'kitchen', Chicago loan). Ezafe 'never receives any degree of stress' (p.444); pronominal enclitics, inflectional suffixes (-ra object marker, -am 'also') and verb affixes are destressed by a general rule (pp.444-446).
